question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

7.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True, because PGS capture is always incomplete due to imperfect LD, winner's curse, and untyped variants, so variance explained is strictly below SNP heritability.

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True—the missing heritability literature shows PGS R² is bounded well below SNP h² by incomplete tagging, winner's curse, and finite power even in large GWAS.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: This is a tricky one that depends on how we define the limits of polygenic scoring in finite samples. I'd like to hear what others think before weighing in.

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance that is explained by the additive effects of all SNPs in the population (i.e., the population \(R^2\) obtained when the phenotype is regressed on every SNP simultaneously). A polygenic score is a linear predictor whose weights are estimated from finite samples; because of estimation error, shrinkage, imperfect tagging, and other statistical losses, its out-of-sample \(R^2\) is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\) except in the theoretical limit of infinite data. Hence the predictive ability of any realizable polygenic score is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability.

8.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by the additive effects of all SNPs in the population (i.e., the theoretical upper bound attainable by any linear SNP-based predictor). A polygenic score is itself a linear combination of SNP genotypes, but its weights are estimated from finite samples; the resulting estimation error, imperfect LD tagging, winner’s-curse bias, and possible shrinkage all ensure that the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by the score is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Equality is reached only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained data—an unattainable condition in practice. Hence the predictive ability of any real polygenic score is necessarily lower than SNP heritability.

The SNP heritability of a phenotype represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that is statistically associated with (i.e., tagged by) the set of measured SNPs; it is the theoretical upper bound on the additive signal that can be captured by any linear combination of those SNPs. A polygenic score is a finite-sample estimate of the optimal SNP weights. Because effect-size estimates contain sampling error, because not every causal variant is perfectly tagged, and because the score is evaluated out-of-sample, the R² achieved by any PGS is strictly less than the SNP heritability (equality is reached only in the unattainable limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained samples with complete causal-variant coverage). Hence the predictive ability of a PGS, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than SNP heritability.

2.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance that is tagged by the set of SNPs (i.e., the additive genetic variance captured by those markers). A polygenic score (PGS) is simply a linear predictor whose weights are estimates of the SNP effect sizes. In the theoretical limit of infinite GWAS sample size, perfect LD between the genotyped/imputed SNPs and the causal variants, and no population stratification or other biases, the estimated weights converge to the true effects; the resulting PGS therefore explains exactly \(h^2_{SNP}\) in an independent sample. Because equality is attainable under these (idealized) conditions, the predictive \(R^2\) of a PGS is not *necessarily* lower than SNP heritability. In practice the two quantities differ because of finite-sample estimation error, imperfect tagging, etc., but the word “necessarily” makes the statement false.

(The same conclusion follows from the fact that \(h^2_{SNP}\) is itself an upper bound on PGS accuracy; an upper bound can be achieved.)

Equality is attained only in the theoretical limit of infinite discovery-sample size, so in any realistic setting the predictive \(R^2\) is necessarily lower.
